paragraphs: This checklist is intended only for self-questioning and does not constitute hiring criteria, a competency score, or an evaluative conclusion about the effectiveness of forestry and conservation work. This page is written according to the United States O*NET-SOC 45-4011.00 "Forest and Conservation Workers" (the fixed index gives this asset the Chinese label meaning "forest and conservation practitioners"; the main subjects are physical-labor work under supervision to develop, maintain, and protect forests, woodlands, wetlands, rangelands, and similar areas, including growing and transporting seedlings, controlling insects, pests, and diseases harmful to plants, and building facilities that control water and soil erosion and seepage; it includes forestry assistants, seedling lifters, tree planters, and gatherers of non-timber forest products such as pine needles).

Paper-based fictional material｜Woodland A plans to plant 120 seedlings; seedling batch S totals 150, of which 18 fail the standards set by the exercise and the rest pass. The issuance log records 115, while the two groups are actually logged at 60 and 55 respectively; another 5 were planted but not logged. Fence facility F has one loose section, tool T is tagged as pending inspection, and notice W suspends all on-site work pending notification from the person in charge. The exercise stipulates: failed seedlings may not be counted as available; logging is by group count with omissions listed separately; tools pending inspection may not be issued; the suspension notice is in force. All fictional; no parameters for agents, burning, or equipment operation are provided. Task｜Within 90 minutes, calculate available seedlings, completed plantings, the shortfall, and inventory; produce the S ledger, the F/T/W exception list, and a handover summary. Inventory means only unused passing seedlings and does not include failed seedlings; completing the record must not be treated as the quarterly survival rate. List to-be-confirmed items as the exercise requires; on-site stoppage is determined by W.

Fit signals｜O*NET points of note: using email every day (97%), face-to-face discussions with individuals and teams every day (78%), being outdoors exposed to all weather every day (70%), telephone communication every day (66%), teamwork being extremely important (52%), continuous contact with others (48%), wearing common protective or safety equipment every day (56%), some freedom to determine tasks and priorities (49%), and some decision-making freedom (56%). If you are willing to complete physical and operational tasks under supervision according to procedures, can work outdoors with a team over the long term, and follow safety requirements, this occupation's daily demands are closer to the way you work.

Caution signals｜O*NET also shows: working indoors in an uncontrolled environment every day (57%), being in an enclosed vehicle or operating enclosed equipment every day (60%), exposure to contaminants more than once a week (53%), exposure to distracting noise more than once a week (45%), exposure to very hot or very cold temperatures more than once a week (44%), exposure to hazardous equipment every day (30%), standing more than half the time (47%), walking or running more than half the time (44%), consequences of error being very serious (36%), and high responsibility for the health and safety of others (41%). Field work carries terrain, weather, wildlife, equipment, and agent risks, and is mostly done in supervised physical labor. If you find long-term outdoor physical labor and seasonal intensity hard to bear, or lack patience for field safety and procedure compliance, treat these as real costs that need careful weighing.

Validation suggestions｜First complete this page's S/F/T/W paper ledger exercise and check the values, record corrections, and suspension status; it cannot validate physical fitness or on-site safety ability. Real job experience must be arranged separately according to employer training and authorization.

Fence facility F has one loose section, tool T is tagged as pending inspection, and notice W suspends all on-site work pending notification from the person in charge. The exercise stipulates: failed seedlings may not be counted as available; logging is by group count with omissions listed separately; tools pending inspection may not be issued; the suspension notice is in force. All fictional; no parameters for agents, burning, or equipment operation are provided. Task｜Within 90 minutes, calculate available seedlings, completed plantings, the shortfall, and inventory; produce the S ledger, the F/T/W exception list, and a handover summary. Inventory means only unused passing seedlings and does not include failed seedlings; completing the record must not be treated as the quarterly survival rate. List to-be-confirmed items as the exercise requires; on-site stoppage is determined by W.

Scope｜O*NET45-4011 covers physical-labor work under supervision to protect and maintain forests, wetlands, and rangelands. Current tasks also include survey assistance, GIS field maps, and procedure explanation or enforcement, and fire prevention and suppression under direction; mapping or firefighting work cannot be categorically excluded; specific design, permitting, enforcement, and fireground command must be checked against real tasks, appointments, and jurisdiction.

entries: Seedling and afforestation work｜Growing and planting｜Prepare and sort seedlings according to the operational design requirements and complete planting and replanting.
Tending and clearing work｜Weeding, thinning, and clearing｜Complete weeding, thinning, and branch and shrub clearing and transport according to the specified marks or specifications.
Facility and camp maintenance｜Roads, fences, and camps｜Build and maintain facilities that control water and erosion, and maintain roads, fences, camps, and recreation-area supplies.

Pest and disease control assistance｜Agent and equipment application｜Under guidance, apply insecticidal or herbicidal agents according to labels and procedures and keep equipment and agents in storage.

Fire prevention and patrol assistance｜Burn management and suppression work｜Under the direction of the fire prevention and suppression lead, carry out burn management, suppression, fireline construction, and fuel clearing.

Survey assistance and rule notification｜Counting, staking, and informing｜Assist the survey crew in clearing survey lines and holding measuring instruments, stake points, and count truthfully, and explain camping, burning, and sanitation rules to users.

paragraphs:
Work context｜O*NET 45-4011.00 work context shows: the work is mainly supervised physical labor, with outdoor work and teamwork standing out.
Communication and collaboration｜Using email every day (97%), face-to-face discussions with individuals and teams every day (78%), teamwork being extremely important (52%), continuous contact with others (48%).

Outdoors and environment｜Being outdoors exposed to all weather every day (70%), working indoors in an uncontrolled environment every day (57%), exposure to very hot or very cold temperatures at least once a week but not every day (44%), being indoors in a controlled environment at least once a week but not every day (31%).

Hazards and protection｜Wearing common protective or safety equipment every day (56%), exposure to hazardous equipment every day (30%), exposure to contaminants at least once a week but not every day (53%), exposure to distracting noise at least once a week but not every day (45%).
Vehicles and equipment｜Being in an enclosed vehicle or operating enclosed equipment every day (60%), telephone communication every day (66%).

Decisions and autonomy｜Some freedom to determine tasks and priorities (49%), some decision-making freedom (56%), making decisions once a month or more but not every week (36%), decisions having an important impact on the results of coworkers and the unit (52%), consequences of error being very serious (36%).
Leadership and responsibility｜Leading or coordinating others being important (35%), high responsibility for the health and safety of others (41%), very high responsibility for the work results of others (33%).

Time and physical effort｜A typical work week of 40 hours (70%), time pressure at least once a month but not every week (46%), standing more than half the time (47%), walking or running more than half the time (44%), using hands to handle, control, or feel objects less than half the time (31%).

Other conditions｜Dealing with external customers or the public being important (40%), writing letters and memos every day (29%), moderate job competition (30%), physical proximity being slightly close (43%). Percentages are the distribution of respondents' answers, not personal work hours or accident rates.

Environment｜70% of respondents report being outdoors in all weather every day, 57% indoors in an uncontrolled environment every day, 44% at least once a week but not every day in hot or cold temperatures, 45% at that frequency for noise, 60% in enclosed vehicles or equipment every day, 30% exposed to hazardous equipment every day; 70% a typical 40-hour week, 46% time pressure at least once a month but not every week, 47% standing more than half the time and 44% walking more than half the time. These are the distribution of answers, not personal work hours. The OOH notes the work is often physically demanding, may involve walking long distances carrying heavy equipment,
and that part-time and seasonal work is common and emergency response may add hours; a specific fire-season intensity is not inferred from the frequency of pressure.

Tools and materials｜Equipment: hand tools for seedlings, planting, weeding, and thinning (shovels, picks, hoes, hand saws, pruning saws), power thinning saws and brush cutters, GPS and compass and survey tape and range poles, field vehicles and all-terrain vehicles, fire prevention and suppression gear and communication equipment, agent application and spraying equipment, and protective equipment (helmets, goggles, gloves, protective clothing, and non-slip boots). Materials: seedlings and seeds and growing medium, herbicidal and pest and disease control agents (stored and applied according to labels and procedures), and fencing
and wire, posts, and marking materials. Documents: operational design and marking files, seedling and planting and thinning specifications, patrol, burning, and sanitation procedures, and safety and emergency processes. All agent use, work, and enforcement judgments must be based on effective versions of the procedures and regulations.

Prepare seedlings and equipment → Plant and weed and thin according to marks → Clear, carry, and pile → Patrol and maintain facilities and camp → Check and store equipment and agents → Record, report, and hand over

Quality suggestions｜Execute and check records according to real design marks, seedling specifications, equipment, and safety procedures; GIS mapping is also a task. For non-urgent design or permit changes, verify authorization; for a direct personal threat, take safety refuge and call and report first, and do not wait for confirmation before stopping dangerous work.

Adjacent responsibility boundaries｜This page covers O*NET-SOC 45-4011.00; adjacent but different occupations include: Forest and Conservation Technicians (responsible for surveys, measurement, mapping, work scheduling, supervision, and leading crews), Foresters (responsible for stand management, harvesting, and long-term planning), Conservation Scientists (responsible for research on natural resources and ecosystems and for management plans), Forest Fire Inspectors and Prevention Specialists (responsible for fire prevention inspections, prevention, and fire-cause investigation), Environmental Science and Protection Technicians, Fish and Game Wardens (responsible for enforcement and patrol), First-Line Supervisors of Farming, Fishing, and Forestry Workers, and Agricultural Technicians. These occupations differ from this one in authorization and outputs; survey design, management decisions, research conclusions, and enforcement discretion are borne by the corresponding roles.

Boundary review points｜Work should be stopped and escalated when the following occur: severe weather and terrain or flood and landslide risk; fire or burn anomalies or an incipient fire; an agent or equipment incident or personal injury; harvesting or work beyond boundaries or in violation of permits and marks; major inconsistencies in counts or records; and conflict or threats involving the public or contractors. The above are handled by the crew and safety lead, the fire prevention and suppression lead, and the competent authority according to regulations and procedures.
Prepare → Plant and tend → Clear and carry → Patrol and maintain → Agents and equipment → Record and report

Comparison｜Workers also include survey assistance and GIS field maps; technicians focus more on data, technical supervision, and leading crews; actual tasks overlap, so boundaries cannot be drawn absolutely based on willingness to do mapping.

Difference from foresters: foresters are responsible for stand management, harvesting, long-term planning, and management decisions and bear the corresponding professional responsibility; this occupation executes specific afforestation, tending, and maintenance work under supervision and does not take part in planning and deciding operations and harvesting.

Core differences from adjacent occupations｜Among the forestry and natural resource roles, responsibility boundaries lie in authorization and outputs: forestry and conservation technicians are responsible for surveys, mapping, work scheduling, and supervision; foresters are responsible for management, harvesting, and long-term planning; conservation scientists are responsible for scientific research and management plans; forest fire inspectors and prevention specialists are responsible for fire prevention inspection, prevention, and fire-cause investigation; environmental science and protection technicians are responsible for environmental sampling and monitoring; fish and game wardens are responsible for enforcement and patrol. This occupation performs physical and operational work under supervision and assists with surveys and facility maintenance; survey design, management decisions, research conclusions, and enforcement discretion must be borne by the corresponding responsible parties.

Difference from environmental-science-and-protection-technicians (environmental science and protection technicians) and forest-fire-inspectors-and-prevention-
specialists (forest fire inspectors and prevention specialists): the former focus on sampling and monitoring environmental media and identifying contamination; the latter focus on fire prevention inspection, prevention, and fire-cause investigation; this occupation centers on executing afforestation, tending, clearing, facility maintenance, and patrol assistance under supervision.

Before choosing this occupation, compare: real tasks (the share of supervised physical and operational work and equipment, agent, and facility maintenance), qualification and training paths (education and on-the-job training and field safety and equipment and agent training), working conditions and responsibility (seasonal and fire-season intensity, outdoor and equipment and agent risks, teamwork and safety requirements), and growth paths (on-site work, skilled and crew-lead roles, or moving toward forestry and conservation technician and first-line supervisor of farming, fishing, and forestry workers, and similar directions). Different
employers (government forestry and natural resource agencies, protected areas and forest farms, forestry and logging and nursery enterprises, and public-interest and nature education organizations) vary considerably and should be checked against actual postings and on-site experience.

Responsibility boundaries cannot be inferred from similarity of job titles: among forestry and natural resource roles, operational execution, survey and mapping, management decisions, scientific research, fire inspection, environmental monitoring, and enforcement differ in authorization and outputs. Working across roles requires relearning procedures, regulations, and safety requirements, and the judgment and sign-off authority of the original role cannot be carried over; survey design, management decisions, research conclusions, and enforcement discretion must be borne by the corresponding responsible parties.

AI task exposure｜Digital tools may assist with organizing and entering seedling and operational records, organizing drone and remote-sensing imagery, patrol routes and hazard registers, GIS and mapping drafts, and drafting operational and outreach materials. But planting, weeding, thinning, clearing, and facility maintenance, equipment and agent use, patrol and burn management, on-site safety, and conflict handling remain the responsibility of workers and crew leads; task exposure does not equal job replacement, and tool output cannot replace field work and verification.

Adoption conditions｜Digital tools entering the work flow must meet: tool output is traceable and reviewable and does not replace judgment about work quality and safety and equipment and agent use; remote-sensing, imagery, and automatic recognition results must undergo field verification and human confirmation before being used in reports and work scheduling; steps involving agent use, burn management, and boundary judgments must not be completed automatically by tools. A technical demonstration does not mean an organization has adopted it, and it does not change operational, safety, or regulatory responsibility.

Data and system thresholds｜Before adoption, verify: whether work, patrol, and count records can be traced back to person, time, place, and equipment; whether coordinates, maps, photos, and database definitions are consistent; the permissions and retention periods for imagery and location data; data consistency and audit trails with work, permitting, and archive systems; and whether offline work can continue and original records be retained during network outages or equipment failures.

Human control points and manual review｜Work execution and quality, equipment and agent use and storage, patrol and burn management and on-site safety, and conflict and incident handling must be completed by workers and crew leads; any tool-generated imagery organization, automatic recognition, statistics, and report drafts must be checked by a human and leave a trail before use.

Residual responsibility｜Matters that must not be released automatically: whether work was completed according to design and marks and meets quality standards, whether equipment and agent use is safe and compliant, whether there is boundary-crossing or permit violation, whether counts and records are truthful, and decisions involving stopping work and reporting. No tool output equals a work conclusion or an authorization decision.

Failure risk｜If tool output is not reviewed, it may lead to inaccurate work scheduling, missed patrols and hazards, imagery misjudgments treated as reality, and distorted counts and records, causing rework and resource, safety, and compliance risks. Before rollout, clarify who reviews and against what source data and field verification.

Employment evidence boundary｜Employment and wage data for this occupation must be distinguished by definition: the United States figures from O*NET and BLS are estimates under a specific statistical definition and cannot be directly extrapolated to mainland China or other regions; China uses the industry-category average wage as a background proxy, which does not constitute an occupational wage conclusion. Everything generated should be traceable to original inputs and sources, and fluent wording must not be treated as correct evidence.

Tool exploration suggestions｜In fictional records, try photo, count, and map assistance and check inputs and correction traces; handle real location, imagery, contract, and forest-right materials according to permissions, and do not treat organizing operations as low risk.

Cross-market definition boundary｜Mainland China and the United States use different industry and occupational classification systems: mainland China publishes average wages of urban unit employees by national economic industry category and does not list this occupation separately; the United States gives estimates by SOC occupation and industry. The two cannot be spliced or converted, and an industry average cannot be used in place of an occupational wage.

Insufficient evidence: this review of the National Bureau of Statistics 2025 urban unit wage release found no mainland China wage or employment value precisely corresponding to this occupation; industry averages are not used as a fill-in.

Mainland China wage evidence review points｜This page provides only statistical definitions, industry background proxies, and a register of visible gaps; it does not provide an estimated salary for this occupation. Before using any value, first confirm whether its statistical definition (industry category / occupation), statistical period, unit of measurement, and covered population are comparable to this occupation.

United States wage evidence review points｜The United States figures on this page come from BLS OEWS May 2025 and the BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook 2025—2035 employment projections (some presented via O*NET). Before use, confirm its occupational scope (SOC 45-4011), whether it includes overtime and seasonal employment and benefits (OEWS excludes benefits), and whether it is a national figure rather than one region or institution.

Mainland China wage evidence — market definition｜The National Bureau of Statistics 2025 industry wages cover urban legal entities with 5 or more persons and exclude self-employed individuals and freelancers, and are not listed separately for this occupation. The agriculture, forestry, animal husbandry, and fishery average can only serve as an industry background; whether a specific job is covered must be checked against the actual employer and survey scope, and must not be presumed from establishment, dispatch, or seasonal status.
Insufficient evidence: no verifiable-by-occupation median wage for forest and conservation workers was obtained for mainland China; the industry-category average is not used as a fill-in.

Mainland China wage evidence — statistical period｜The industry average wage is an annual figure (the values below are for 2025, released in 2026) and differs from the May 2025 point-in-time wage for the United States on this page; the two periods cannot be mixed.

Cross-market definition boundary｜Mainland China's industry average wage and the United States' occupational wage differ in statistical object, period, and definition; this page lists them separately with limitations noted, makes no currency conversion, and does not treat the industry average as an occupational wage.

Mainland China wage evidence — unit of measurement｜The National Bureau of Statistics publishes pre-tax annual average wages in yuan per year, and total wages include wages, bonuses, allowances and subsidies, and items stipulated as included; the items included in OEWS pre-tax wages for normal hours differ, so the two are not directly comparable.

Insufficient evidence: no wage data for forest and conservation workers verifiable by region or employment form was obtained for mainland China; individual quotes or secondhand accounts are not used as a fill-in.

Mainland China wage evidence — covered population｜The 2025 statistics cover urban legal entities with 5 or more persons and exclude self-employed individuals and freelancers; whether an actual employer falls within the survey scope should be checked, and temporary workers must not be categorically excluded based on status.

United States wage evidence — market definition｜OEWS is an employer wage sample estimate covering full-time and part-time wage and salary employees and excluding the self-employed; the median is the midpoint of the distribution, not a starting wage.

United States wage evidence — statistical period｜Wages are May 2025 OEWS; employment and growth are the 2025—2035 employment projections (openings based on the BLS OOH 2025—2035 annual average). The two types of data have different reference points and must not be mixed into a single point-in-time conclusion.

United States wage evidence — unit of measurement｜OEWS annual wages are usually converted as hourly wage ×2,080 hours, an all-year full-time statistical assumption; it cannot replace the actual paid hours and annual income of seasonal employees.

United States wage evidence — covered population｜OEWS includes full-time and part-time wage and salary employees within the survey scope and should not broadly exclude seasonal short-term workers; the self-employed, unincorporated business owners, and partners are outside that survey scope.

United States wage evidence — occupational scope｜The values on this page correspond to SOC 45-4011 (Forest and Conservation Workers); they exclude Forest and Conservation Technicians (19-4071), Foresters (19-1032), Conservation Scientists (19-1031), Forest Fire Inspectors and Prevention Specialists (33-2022), Environmental Science and Protection Technicians (19-4042), Fish and Game Wardens (33-3031), First-Line Supervisors of Farming, Fishing, and Forestry Workers (45-1011), Agricultural Technicians (19-4012), and Loggers (45-4021). Wages cannot be mixed across occupations. 45-4021 is Fallers and 45-4022 is Logging Equipment Operators; logging workers are a collection of several SOC codes.

The current May2025 national profile and the profiles of three specific industries have been read successfully, covering OEWS6050 employees; OOH14700 positions include the self-employed. The selected state government figure is 43680, local government 40150, and business, professional, labor, political, and similar organizations 56800, while the OOH composite for religious, grantmaking, civic, professional, and similar organizations is 39590; the detailed category compositions differ, and no estimate is made for industries not selected.

Conclusion｜The core difference between this occupation and adjacent occupations lies in authorization and outputs: this occupation performs physical and operational work such as planting, tending, clearing, and facility maintenance under supervision and assists with surveys and truthful counting; forestry and conservation technicians handle surveys, measurement, mapping, work scheduling, supervision, and leading crews; foresters are responsible for stand management, harvesting, and long-term planning; conservation scientists are responsible for scientific research and management plans; forest fire inspectors and prevention specialists are responsible for fire prevention inspection, prevention, and fire-cause investigation
; environmental science and protection technicians are responsible for sampling and monitoring environmental media. Authorization and outputs differ in each case, so judgment and sign-off authority cannot be carried across roles.

Evidence note｜The comparison subjects in the table below come from the O*NET occupational classification and official public task materials and are used to help distinguish the work content of adjacent occupations and to support fit choices; they do not constitute qualification, hiring, or pay conclusions. The wages and employment of each occupation must be checked separately under their own SOC definition; this table makes no numerical comparison and does not treat one occupation's wage as a proxy for another.

Preface｜The following comparison is laid out in four columns: occupational direction — core work and outputs — key differences — who it suits better. These forestry and natural resource field positions are often sequenced by season and operations, but sequencing does not mean they are interchangeable; when moving across directions, procedures, regulations, and safety and qualification requirements must be relearned.

Centers on executing physical work such as afforestation, tending, clearing, and facility maintenance under supervision and assisting with surveys and truthful counting: seedling preparation and planting and replanting; weeding, thinning, and branch and shrub clearing and transport; road, fence, and camp maintenance; applying and storing agents and equipment under guidance; and taking part in burn management, suppression, and fireline construction under direction.

Better suited to people who are willing to complete physical and operational tasks outdoors over the long term according to procedures and instructions, can comply with safety management, and record truthfully.

Outputs are completed operational tasks and verifiable records: planting, tending, and clearing records; equipment and agent use and protection records; patrol and facility and camp maintenance records; and count and survey-line assistance records during survey support.
This occupation: Forest and Conservation Workers

Centers on survey, tending, patrol, and operational supervision of stands, soil, water resources, and habitat: plot selection, measurement, and recording; mapping and database entry; scheduling and quality supervision of thinning, weeding, and replanting; patrol, burn management, and fire prevention outreach; and leading crews and public education.

Better suited to people who take responsibility for surveys, measurement, mapping, work scheduling, and supervision; this occupation executes work under their direction and assists with surveys and counting.

Outputs are usable resource data and operational results: plot and survey records; stand, mapping, and database products; operational and acceptance records for tending and replanting; and patrol, fire prevention outreach, and exception records.
Forest and Conservation Technicians
Centers on stand management, harvesting, and long-term planning: management plans and harvest design; stand growth, regeneration, and benefit analysis; and management and permit decisions.

Better suited to people who take responsibility for management and harvest decisions and professional accountability; this occupation executes afforestation, tending, and maintenance work under their direction and that of technicians.
Outputs are management and harvest plans: management and operational design documents; stand growth and benefit analyses; and harvest, regeneration, and acceptance conclusions.
Foresters

Centers on scientific research and management plans for natural resources and ecosystems: ecological and resource surveys and modeling; design of conservation and restoration plans; and monitoring, evaluation, and publication.
Better suited to people who take responsibility for research and plan design; this occupation provides operational execution and basic data assistance.
Outputs are research and plan results: survey, modeling, and monitoring results; restoration and management plans; and evaluation and publication.
Conservation Scientists

Centers on fire prevention inspection, prevention, and fire-cause investigation: fuel, facility, and burn inspections; fire prevention outreach and prevention plans; and fire-cause investigation and reporting.

Better suited to people whose professional direction is fire prevention inspection, prevention, and fire-cause investigation; this occupation takes part in burn management, suppression, and fireline construction under the direction of the fire prevention lead.
Outputs are fire prevention inspection and prevention conclusions: inspection and hazard remediation records; fire prevention outreach and plan documents; and fire-cause investigation and reports.
Forest Fire Inspectors and Prevention Specialists

Centers on sampling and monitoring environmental media and identifying contamination: sampling and analysis of water, soil, air, and biological samples; monitoring networks and data management; and environmental impact and contamination identification.
Better suited to people who focus on environmental sampling, monitoring, and contamination identification; this occupation is mainly supervised afforestation, tending, and maintenance work.
Outputs are environmental monitoring results: sampling and analysis records; monitoring data and reports; and contamination identification and remediation recommendations.
Environmental Science and Protection Technicians

Selection suggestions｜Compare actual tasks and outputs, then check recruitment, education, training, and permissions. The OOH lists possible moves toward technician and forester directions, but this occupation is not a required entry level for all forestry roles; promotion and role changes require meeting the target requirements separately.

What kind of personality suits it? This occupation values responsibility, safety and procedural awareness, and teamwork more than any personality type; the O*NET interest code is RC (Realistic—Conventional), which can serve as a starting point for exploration.

Are introverted people suited? This cannot be judged from an introversion or extraversion label alone. O*NET reports 78% for face-to-face discussions every day and 52% for teamwork being extremely important; first check the actual communication tasks and your own experience.

The United States OOH notes the work is often physically demanding and may involve walking long distances carrying heavy equipment and working in remote areas; 70% of respondents report being outdoors in all weather every day, which does not equal the probability of lodging. Most work is full-time, part-time and seasonal work is common, and emergency response may extend hours; the specific fire-season intensity, lodging, training, and health requirements should be checked by job.

Where does everyday pressure mainly come from? Consequences of error being very serious (36%), working indoors in an uncontrolled environment every day (57%), exposure to contaminants at least once a week but not every day (53%), exposure to very hot or very cold temperatures at least once a week but not every day (44%), noise at least once a week but not every day (45%), and high responsibility for the health and safety of others (41%). Percentages are the distribution of respondents' answers, not personal work hours or accident rates.

47% report standing more than half the time and 44% walking more than half the time, which is a respondent distribution; the OOH describes possibly walking long distances carrying heavy equipment, which does not mean everyone carries loads every day. Check specific employer postings.

Will doing this long term harm the body? Field, weather, terrain, equipment, agent, and animal risks and the musculoskeletal burden of repetitive motions, load carrying, and prolonged standing are real costs; protective equipment should be used according to procedures and occupational health and fitness management done well.

Career cycle and transition directions? You can grow from seasonal worker and operational assistant to skilled and crew-lead worker, or move toward forestry and conservation technician and first-line supervisor of farming, fishing, and forestry workers, and similar directions; crossing directions requires relearning procedures and education and qualification requirements.

paragraphs: Boundary｜What this page lists are the more common failure types and control points for this occupation in supervised afforestation, tending, and patrol work, intended to help identify and manage risk; it does not constitute legal, operational safety, fire, agent use, occupational health, or resource management advice. Anything involving fire and casualties, equipment and agent incidents, boundary-crossing and permit violations, and enforcement disputes should be handled by the person in charge, the safety and fire leads, and the competent authority according to regulations and procedures.

Direct answer｜The core risk of this occupation is not "can you do the work" but four types of failure with heavier consequences: field and operational safety failure (terrain and weather and floods and falls and equipment and vehicle accidents), fire and burn failure (burn management and suppression and smoking and machinery ignition risk), work quality and record failure (planting, sorting, counting, and record errors and rework), and compliance and conflict failure (boundary-crossing and violation of burn and sanitation procedures and agent and equipment violations and conflicts with the public or contractors).

Evidence scope｜The risk premises take the United States O*NET tasks and environment and the OOH outdoor physical work and training notes; the scenarios, consequences, and check actions below are editorial examples, not incidence rates, medical causation, or Chinese statutory safe-operating rules.
Workers and crew leads; crew members and oneself

Working on steep slopes or slippery terrain or in severe weather or flood and lightning conditions, or improper use of equipment and vehicles; personal injury such as falls and falls from height and vehicle and equipment injuries and hypothermia and heatstroke

Adjust work to weather and terrain conditions and provide full protection and communications, and prohibit entering high-risk areas alone; if weather or terrain deteriorates, stop work, withdraw, and report immediately
Scenario｜Work continued as planned under continuous rain and steep-slope conditions, and one worker slipped and was injured on a wet slope.
Workers and crew members; crew members and the public and forest resources
Burn management not in place, or equipment and vehicles igniting, or smoking and open flames uncontrolled; fire occurrence and spread, endangering people and resource safety

China 2026 regulations｜Report a fire immediately and secure refuge first; anyone without professional training must not be assigned to fight it directly, and participation must follow unified command. This page provides no suppression operating parameters; the specific fire prevention zone, period, and burn permit should be checked against current local rules.
Scenario｜During the fire season, equipment with an open flame was used at the woodland edge without clearing the ignition source, and after leaving, smoldering started a fire.
Workers and crew leads and technicians; work quality and resource management

Planting, weeding, thinning, and clearing do not meet specifications, or seedling sorting and counting and records are untrue; survival rates and work quality decline with rework, and resource data and settlement are distorted

Work according to marks and specifications and accept crew-lead verification; counts and records must be truthful and not overstated; report immediately and redo or correct when specification mismatches or counting anomalies are found
Scenario｜Different crews planted and counted by different definitions without verification, and the survival rate and settlement data differed sharply from reality.
Workers and contractors and the public; resources and institutions and individuals

Harvesting or work beyond boundaries or in violation of permits and marks, or conflict and threats involving the public or contractors; resource loss and compliance and legal disputes and personal safety risk

Define boundaries according to permits and marks and leave a trail; in conflict, keep communicating, stop work, and await authorization; for boundary-crossing and threats, withdraw immediately and report and refer to enforcement
Scenario｜A contractor worked beyond the boundary, and the worker only verbally discouraged them without stopping work and reporting, so the boundary dispute could not be defined afterwards.
Workers and crew members; oneself and others
Improper storage, application, or maintenance of agents and equipment, or inadequate protection; poisoning and burns and cuts and equipment injuries and environmental contamination

Store, apply, and maintain according to labels and procedures and provide full protection and decontamination, and record amounts and batches; in case of a leak or exposure, handle according to emergency procedures, seek medical care, and report immediately
Scenario｜A herbicidal agent was not diluted according to the label and no protection was worn; a worker suffered skin burns and there were no decontamination facilities on site.
Workers and crew members and facilities; oneself and the public and facilities

Long hours of physical work and load carrying and repetitive motions and prolonged standing, or risks in camp, road, fence, and equipment maintenance; musculoskeletal strain and fatigue-related errors and work injuries and facility damage

Arrange rotation and rest breaks reasonably and prepare physically, and inspect camps, facilities, and equipment according to procedures; report immediately and adjust work when persistent discomfort or facility hazards appear
Scenario｜After several consecutive days of long-distance hiking and load-carrying work without rotation, one crew member made an operating error while driving back.

Seedling and condition materials

Paper-based fictional material｜Woodland A plans to plant 120 seedlings; seedling batch S totals 150, of which 18 fail the standards set by the exercise and the rest pass. The issuance log records 115, while the two groups are actually logged at 60 and 55 respectively; another 5 were planted but not logged. Fence facility F has one loose section, tool T is tagged as pending inspection, and notice W suspends all on-site work pending notification from the person in charge. The exercise stipulates: failed seedlings may not be counted as available; logging is by group count with omissions listed separately; tools pending inspection may not
be issued; the suspension notice is in force. All fictional; no parameters for agents, burning, or equipment operation are provided.
The exercise rules are valid only for this practice and are not an industry standard.
Calculation and handover task

Task｜Within 90 minutes, calculate available seedlings, completed plantings, the shortfall, and inventory; produce the S ledger, the F/T/W exception list, and a handover summary. Inventory means only unused passing seedlings and does not include failed seedlings; completing the record must not be treated as the quarterly survival rate. List to-be-confirmed items as the exercise requires; on-site stoppage is determined by W.
Deliver the ledger, the exception list, and the summary; do not guess survival data that was not provided.
Recomputable reference deliverable

Reference calculation｜Available 150−18=132 seedlings; actually planted 60+55+5=120 seedlings; the original log of 115 must have the 5 omitted seedlings added with correction traces kept; the plan shortfall is 120−120=0 seedlings, and unused passing seedlings are 132−120=12. The 18 failed seedlings are listed separately, and the total check is 120+12+18=150. W is still in force, and work cannot resume just because the task quantity is met; T pending inspection goes to the person in charge, and the loose F is logged and reported. No later survival
data was provided, so the survival rate cannot be calculated.
Keep the formula, units, and reason for each correction item by item against the material.
Paper exercise boundaries

Boundary｜This is an editor-designed paper record exercise. It judges only the given counts and statuses, does not perform planting, agents, open flames, power equipment, or on-site surveys, and does not sign off on work quality; resumption, tool acceptance, and fence repair are decided by the truly authorized person in charge according to actual rules.
S seedling ledger
List the 150 total, 18 failed, 132 available, 120 planted, and 12 remaining; keep the original log of 115 and the +5 correction source, and do not change the original record.

Fence F loose, tool T pending inspection and not issuable, notice W suspension still in force; write the responsible person to confirm each, and the suspension cannot be lifted by meeting the quantity.
Handover summary
Hand over the 120 planned and 120 actual seedlings, the 12 remaining, the 5 omitted and corrected, and the three statuses; there is no survival data, so no survival rate is reported.
Recalculation and tool notes
Check 120+12+18=150 by hand; if a tool takes part in record organizing, mark the inputs, outputs, and differences from human verification. A paper deliverable is not evidence of on-site competence.

entries.answer:
According to O*NET-SOC 45-4011.00, this occupation performs the physical labor needed to develop, maintain, and protect forests, woodlands, wetlands, rangelands, and similar areas under supervision, including growing and transporting seedlings, controlling insects, pests, and diseases harmful to plants, and building facilities that control water and soil erosion and seepage; it includes forestry assistants, seedling lifters, tree planters, and non-timber forest product gatherers. The work includes seedling preparation and planting and replanting, weeding and thinning and branch and shrub clearing and transport, road and fence and camp maintenance, applying and storing agents and equipment under
guidance, taking part in burn management and suppression and fireline construction under direction, assisting the survey crew in clearing survey lines and holding measuring instruments and staking and counting truthfully, and explaining camping, burning, and sanitation rules to users. It does not independently bear survey design, quality supervision and management planning decisions, stand management and harvest and long-term planning decisions, scientific research and plan formulation, fire prevention inspection and prevention and fire-cause investigation, environmental media sampling and monitoring, independent logging
positions focused on harvesting and hauling, or the final determination of permitting and enforcement and legal application.
entries.question: What does this occupation actually do?

entries.answer:
Forestry and conservation technicians handle surveys, measurement, mapping, databases, work scheduling, supervision, and leading crews; foresters are responsible for stand management and harvesting and long-term planning and bear professional decision responsibility; conservation scientists are responsible for scientific research and management plans for natural resources and ecosystems; forest fire inspectors and prevention specialists are responsible for fire prevention inspection, prevention, and fire-cause investigation; environmental science and protection technicians are responsible for sampling and monitoring environmental media; fish and game wardens are responsible for enforcement and patrol. This occupation
performs physical and operational work such as planting, tending, clearing, and facility maintenance under supervision and assists with surveys and truthful counting.

entries.answer:
Common failures include: steep slopes and slippery terrain and severe weather and equipment and vehicle accidents, burn and ignition and fire risk, planting, sorting, counting, and record errors and rework, boundary-crossing or violation of burn and sanitation procedures and conflicts with the public or contractors, improper storage, application, and maintenance of agents and equipment, and the health effects of long hours of physical work and load carrying and repetitive motions. The control points are to execute according to procedures and operational design requirements and leave a trail, and to stop work, withdraw, report, and refer according to procedures; matters involving
fire, boundary-crossing, enforcement, and accidents are handled by the person in charge and the competent authority.
